publication_type: Topic-level evidence synthesis combining peer-reviewed school monitoring studies, IoT platform papers, AI and automation reviews, and operational guidance from live district dashboard programs.
country_and_climate: The evidence base is multi-country and multi-climate. It includes Boston Public Schools in the northeastern United States with a cold-humid temperate climate, Portuguese classroom deployments in Atlantic and Mediterranean-influenced settings, and Italian school control concepts in a Mediterranean climate. This matters because alert thresholds, outdoor-baseline handling, window-opening feasibility, and automation trade-offs depend strongly on season, weather, and building type.
objective_and_research_question: The main objective is to turn continuous classroom IEQ and IAQ sensing into operational action. The recurring research question is not only how to measure CO2, particles, temperature, humidity, and related variables, but how to aggregate them into dashboards, persistence-based alerts, room rankings, maintenance priorities, and in some cases semi-automated or automated ventilation responses that school staff can actually use.
study_design: The literature is methodologically mixed. It includes district-scale longitudinal monitoring with decision-support visualizations, multi-room IoT architecture and control concept papers, proof-of-concept school deployments, hardware-focused classroom pilots, and recent reviews of AI-enabled prediction and control. Most evidence is observational or engineering-evaluative rather than randomized.
educational_context: The dominant context is K-12 classrooms, with some higher-education spaces used for proof-of-concept and method development. The relevant rooms are densely occupied teaching spaces with recurring schedules, strong room-to-room heterogeneity, and either natural ventilation, central mechanical ventilation, or mixed-mode operation. Dashboards are most useful where facilities teams must triage many rooms rather than inspect one room at a time.
sample_and_duration: The strongest operational case study is Boston Public Schools, where 3,659 classroom sensors in 125 buildings generated 245 million CO2 measurements over the 2022-2023 school year. Complementary evidence includes SchoolAIR pilot deployment in university classrooms with proof of concept in a high school in northern Portugal, and Smart Healthy Schools validation in an Italian school. Across the broader educational AI review, the evidence spans twenty real-world case studies from multiple regions.
environmental_variables: Dashboards and rule engines most commonly rely on indoor CO2, PM2.5, PM10, air temperature, relative humidity, and where available outdoor baseline measurements. Some programs also track CO, illuminance, environmental noise, occupancy metadata, and building-operation context. For decision support, the most useful derived metrics are time above thresholds, peak events, occupied-period percentiles, recovery after vacancy, and room-to-room comparisons.
outdoor_conditions_and_baseline: Outdoor context is essential. Boston Public Schools reports a roof-top unit at every school to establish an outdoor baseline per location, and classroom interpretation becomes much more robust when outdoor CO2, particles, and weather are available. Without this context, a dashboard may trigger the wrong action, especially when natural ventilation would import outdoor pollution, noise, heat, or cold.
occupancy_and_activity: Dashboards are only meaningful when aligned to classroom schedules and occupancy patterns. Lesson periods, breaks, class turnover, cleaning, gym or lab activities, vocal intensity, and manual overrides all change the signal. A practical rule engine therefore needs occupied-state tagging, timetable integration, or at least an occupied-hour mask so that alerts are based on relevant exposure windows rather than overnight or weekend behavior.
ventilation_and_filtration_operation: The literature consistently treats windows, doors, HVAC outdoor-air fraction, purge cycles, exhaust operation, and portable filtration as core state variables for decision-making. District operational pages from Boston Public Schools also describe continuous fan operation, pre- and post-occupancy flushing, air purifiers, and thermal-setpoint adjustments. Dashboards are most valuable when they distinguish interventions that affect CO2 through outdoor-air renewal from those that affect particles without reducing CO2, such as HEPA filtration.
spatial_granularity: Room-level sensing is the minimum defensible granularity for operational dashboards because classroom conditions vary substantially within and between schools. A practical architecture is one fixed sensor per regularly occupied classroom plus one outdoor reference per building or campus cluster. Building-level averages are still useful for portfolio oversight, but they can hide high-exposure outlier rooms that drive health, comfort, and maintenance risk.
sensor_specification: Dashboard and automation programs should be built on true CO2 sensors using NDIR or photoacoustic NDIR, paired with reliable T/RH sensing and either PM2.5 alone or PM1 plus PM2.5 plus PM10 depending on the use case. If noise and light are included, they should be treated as separate IEQ channels rather than folded blindly into IAQ logic. Optional occupancy channels are best added through schedule integration, PIR, or mmWave rather than inferred only from CO2 if the dashboard will trigger strong actions.
calibration_and_qaqc: Operational trust depends on QA/QC more than on visualization polish. The recurring good practice is pre-deployment collocation, timestamp control, warm-up handling, documented calibration state, review of flatlines and spikes, outdoor background checks, and explicit management of automatic baseline correction for CO2 sensors. Public-facing dashboards should also surface QA flags so school staff can distinguish poor air conditions from suspect instrumentation.
acquisition_and_data_quality: A common pattern is minute-scale collection with 15-minute rolling averages or medians for public display and alerts. Boston Public Schools uses public-facing 15-minute rolling values, while the underlying analytics work from minute-level histories. For school operations, uptime, buffering through outages, clock consistency, and clear treatment of missing data are as important as nominal sensor accuracy because false alerts quickly erode trust.
sensor_lifecycle: [uncertain] Lifecycle performance depends heavily on the chosen channels and the maintenance program. CO2 and T/RH channels are usually multi-year, while PM modules, fans, optional gas channels, and occupancy peripherals carry higher maintenance burden. In real dashboard programs, field failures, network dropout, and neglected recalibration usually create more operational trouble than immediate sensor end-of-life.
recommended_sensor_by_variable: For dashboard-driven school operations, the preferred stack is true CO2 by NDIR or photoacoustic NDIR, direct T/RH sensing, and PM2.5 or PM1 plus PM2.5 optical particle sensing with transparent caveats about aerosol dependence. Add PM10 only as a secondary indicator, lux only if lighting decisions are in scope, calibrated noise metrics only if acoustic management is needed, and direct occupancy metadata if the rules engine depends on occupied-state precision. Avoid eCO2-only sensors for ventilation alerts and avoid treating MOS VOC indexes as equivalent to pollutant concentration limits.
useful_output_and_units: The outputs that support decisions best are CO2 in ppm, PM fractions in micrograms per cubic meter, air temperature in degrees C, RH in percent, occupied-time above thresholds in minutes or percent, 15-minute rolling values for public display, and room-level status labels such as normal, warning, or high. If a composite room-priority score is used, the underlying raw units must remain visible.
direct_measurement_or_proxy: A robust dashboard must preserve the distinction between direct measurements and proxies. True CO2, T/RH, PM optical counts and masses, lux, and acoustic levels are direct measured channels, even if some of them require calibration. Ventilation adequacy, infection-risk implication, occupancy inference, room-priority ranking, and maintenance urgency are derived products that depend on assumptions and aggregation rules.
measurement_principle_and_selectivity: True CO2 should come from selective NDIR or photoacoustic NDIR sensing. PM comes from optical scattering and therefore depends on aerosol composition. T/RH uses mature digital environmental sensing. Lux comes from photopic light sensing and noise from MEMS microphone pressure capture with edge signal processing. Occupancy can be coarse via PIR or finer via mmWave. These principle differences matter because rules should trust selective channels more than broad-response or inferred channels.
useful_range_and_real_performance: For school dashboards, sensors should remain credible from clean-room baseline to severe event conditions rather than merely meet nominal catalog ranges. In Boston Public Schools, the average school-day CO2 concentration was 841 ppm with a standard deviation of 405 ppm and peaks up to 5,080 ppm, so saturation near ordinary action levels would be unacceptable. Public dashboards also need smoothing and persistence logic because perfectly raw high-frequency traces are often too noisy for action.
operating_regime: The preferred regime is always-on room sensing, local buffering, and minute-scale transmission, with edge or cloud aggregation into 15-minute public values and longer analytical windows for trend detection. Alerting should include persistence so that a single spike does not trigger unnecessary action. For automation, control intervals should be long enough to avoid oscillation and short enough to respond during the same occupied period.
interferences_and_confounders: Key confounders are poor sensor placement, direct solar exposure, drafts, stratification, changing outdoor baseline, irregular schedules, incomplete occupancy metadata, network outages, and user behavior such as sporadic window opening. A second class of confounder is semantic: users may read a dashboard color as a diagnosis of safety when it is only a screening indicator. This is especially risky when CO2 is used as a proxy for broader IAQ.
affordable_validation_protocol: A practical TCC-scale validation path is to deploy at least two duplicate classroom nodes, collocate them with one better reference per core variable for 7 to 14 days, then run a pilot in one or more classrooms for 2 to 4 weeks with an event log. Validate not only channel accuracy but also alert logic, buffering, time synchronization, and whether recommended interventions actually align with observed room behavior. If automation is added, test the control rules in shadow mode before allowing real actuation.
validation_metrics: Minimum metrics are bias, MAE, RMSE, slope and intercept versus a better reference, uptime, missing-data fraction, false-alert frequency, and latency from threshold exceedance to dashboard update. For decision support, add persistence-hit rates, proportion of alerts that led to a verified intervention, and whether room rankings remain stable when using alternative averaging windows. For automated control, report overshoot, oscillation frequency, and energy or runtime penalty.
installation_and_enclosure: Classroom monitors should be placed near the breathing zone, away from windows, doors, supply jets, corners, direct breath plumes, and heat-producing electronics. Enclosures should be ventilated and should keep PM inlets, acoustic ports, and thermal sensors functionally exposed. If one node is expected to support dashboarding, alerting, and automation, installation metadata such as room ID, height, orientation, and nearby ventilation features must be recorded because the rule logic depends on them.
hardware_integration: A common architecture is an ESP32- or gateway-linked node with I2C or UART sensors, local flash or SD buffering, and Wi-Fi, LoRaWAN, or other campus connectivity. The integration challenge is less about reading a sensor and more about maintaining synchronized timestamps, stable firmware, retry behavior, and secure uplink to a time-series backend that can feed dashboards, notifications, and maintenance systems.
total_implementation_cost: [uncertain] Program cost is usually dominated by deployment scale, networking, maintenance labor, and dashboard operations rather than by one sensor channel. A modest per-room monitoring node can be affordable, but a district-grade dashboard program also needs cloud services, calibration checks, device replacement stock, user support, and staff time for interpretation and response. As of 2026-08-11, the most defensible statement is that the software and operations layer is often underestimated relative to the hardware bill of materials.
evidence_maturity: Evidence maturity is strong for room-level dashboarding, trend visualization, and exposure triage based on continuous sensing, especially for CO2-centered ventilation management. It is moderate for cross-variable alert logic, moderate for district-scale maintenance prioritization, and only low-to-moderate for fully automated classroom actuation that remains robust across seasons and building types. AI-enabled prediction is promising but still less mature than straightforward rules plus transparent visualization.
variable_specific_cautions: Do not treat CO2 as a complete IAQ score. Do not treat particle alerts without outdoor context as proof of an indoor source. Do not fold proxy variables and direct variables into a single color without exposing uncertainty. Avoid retaining intelligible audio if acoustic channels are used. If occupancy is inferred instead of measured, do not make high-stakes automation depend on that inference alone.
system_architecture: The most defensible architecture is node to campus network to message broker or HTTPS ingestion to time-series database to analytics and rule engine to dashboard and notification layer. Mature versions add outdoor baseline nodes, QA metadata, device-health monitoring, and optional links to BMS or CMMS tools so that a persistent room problem can generate a maintenance workflow rather than remain a graph on a screen.
connectivity_and_protocols: Wi-Fi with MQTT or HTTPS is the simplest fit where school infrastructure already exists, while LoRaWAN is attractive for lower-power or harder-to-wire retrofits and is explicitly featured in Smart Healthy Schools. The protocol choice should reflect network policy, reliability, telemetry frequency, and maintenance capacity. Rule execution can live in the cloud, at the edge gateway, or partly on the node depending on latency and resilience requirements.
interoperability_and_data_model: A useful schema includes timestamp, room ID, school ID, device ID, measured variable, unit, occupied-state tag, QA flag, firmware version, and baseline source. To support automation and maintenance, the same data model should also expose rule outputs such as alert severity, intervention recommendation, acknowledgment state, and work-order linkage. Open JSON or CSV structures are enough for a TCC, but Brick or Haystack style metadata make later institutional scaling easier.
cybersecurity_privacy_and_ethics: Room-level environmental data can reveal classroom schedules, occupancy habits, and operational weaknesses even when no personal identifiers are stored. Authentication, encrypted transport, device identity control, and role-based access are therefore necessary. If the system includes occupancy sensing, acoustic summaries, or automated control, privacy and governance requirements rise sharply. The safest baseline is no raw audio retention, no camera dependence, and clear disclosure that the system monitors rooms rather than individuals.
analytical_methods: Typical methods are rolling averages, persistence filters, occupied-period masking, room ranking by exposure burden, anomaly detection, simple forecasting, and intervention tracking. More advanced work adds machine learning for pollutant forecasting, air-exchange estimation, fault detection, and prioritization of maintenance action. In practice, dashboards perform best when the primary analytics stay interpretable and the AI layer remains assistive rather than opaque.
derived_index_or_model: A practical derived model is a room-priority score that combines direct measurements, persistence, and context. For example, repeated occupied CO2 exceedance, slow post-class recovery, elevated PM during occupancy, and sustained RH problems can be aggregated into a triage score for facilities teams. More advanced variants can add rebreathed-fraction estimates, infection-risk proxies, or predictive risk horizons, but these should remain secondary overlays rather than hidden replacements for raw signals.
decision_rules_and_standards: Operational decision rules should combine threshold values with persistence and context. The 2025 USGBC school IAQ toolkit cites Boston Public Schools using CO2 above 2,000 ppm as high on a 15-minute average and RH above 60 percent as high on a 15-minute average, while other districts cite lower aspirational CO2 bands such as below 1,200 ppm for proper ventilation and cognitive support. A robust classroom rule library therefore uses traffic-light bands, persistence windows, occupied-state filtering, and variable-specific comments instead of pretending one universal threshold applies everywhere.
intervention_and_automation: The most common interventions are manual or supervised: open windows when outdoor air is favorable, increase outdoor-air delivery, extend purge cycles, dispatch maintenance, move portable HEPA units, or change room use. Automation is possible at several levels: notify the teacher, trigger the building operator, adjust windows or HVAC setpoints, or run predictive control based on expected occupancy and weather. Current evidence supports simple supervised automation more strongly than fully autonomous actuation in ordinary school portfolios.
environmental_outcomes: The clearest environmental outcome is earlier detection of problematic rooms and more defensible prioritization of ventilation or filtration actions. Boston Public Schools used classroom-level visualizations to identify high-exposure rooms, and district materials report public transparency and operational changes linked to monitoring. Across the literature, dashboards and alerts improve observability first, and improvements in IEQ follow when the organization has the capacity to act on that observability.
health_and_learning_outcomes: [uncertain] The evidence that dashboards alone produce direct health or learning gains is still indirect. The more defensible claim is that actionable room-level monitoring can reduce exposure to conditions associated with poorer comfort, symptom burden, and degraded attention, provided that alerts actually lead to ventilation or maintenance action. Strong causal evidence linking dashboard deployment alone to student outcomes remains limited.
objective_subjective_integration: Measured data and human perception should be used together but not treated as equivalent. School studies already show that teacher perception does not always match monitored conditions. Dashboards therefore benefit from simple annotation channels for stuffiness, unusual noise, or thermal discomfort, while still grounding decisions in measured trends and QA-screened data.
quantitative_results: The most policy-relevant quantitative result is from Boston Public Schools: 3,659 classroom sensors across 125 buildings produced 245 million CO2 measurements during the 2022-2023 school year, with an average school-day CO2 of 841 ppm, a standard deviation of 405 ppm, and daily peaks up to 5,080 ppm. USGBC district materials also report that measured classroom CO2 concentrations were below 1,000 ppm about 75 percent of the time during school hours on average in that program. These numbers show both the scale of modern school dashboarding and the need for room-level triage rather than one building average.
feasibility_and_acceptance: Feasibility is high for traffic-light dashboards and moderate for multi-variable alerting tied to maintenance workflow. Acceptance is best when alerts map cleanly to concrete actions and when staff can see that the system improves room conditions rather than audits individual behavior. The biggest organizational barriers are weak metadata, unplanned maintenance workload, and unclear ownership of alert response, not the existence of low-cost sensors.
validity_and_limitations: Dashboards compress a complex indoor environment into human-actionable cues, which is exactly their strength and their limitation. Thresholds may not transfer across climates, ventilation modes, or school policies. Raw sensor uncertainty, smoothing windows, occupancy assumptions, and missing outdoor context can all distort alert meaning. Any automation layer must therefore remain transparent about its assumptions and should fail safely when data quality drops.
contribution_and_research_gaps: The literature now supports a practical pathway from school sensing to action: room-level monitoring, baseline-aware dashboards, persistence-based alerts, and explicit mapping from alerts to facilities or ventilation actions. The main gaps are standardized school alert libraries, better cross-variable fusion rules, stronger interoperability with BMS and maintenance systems, and outcome studies that quantify how much monitoring plus dashboarding actually improves ventilation equity, comfort, health, and educational performance.
